profiles.meeting_scenario: A design review is being held at a university hospital's translational medicine center for an existing proposal called 'StrideCue,' an ankle-worn cueing device intended to reduce freezing episodes in people with Parkinson's disease during daily walking at home. The device team has already completed bench testing and a small supervised usability study, and now needs to decide whether the current design and pilot plan are ready for presentation to the hospital innovation board and, if endorsed, a regional medtech industry consortium that may support commercialization. The agenda is to review the proposed home-use pilot, the evidence package on safety and usability, the way quality-of-life benefit will be captured, and the summary slides that cite prior caregiver input. The expected outcome is a go/no-go decision on whether the package is 'board-ready' with minor edits, plus a short list of revisions each participant believes are needed before submission.

members.name: Dr. Neha Raman
members.expertise: Movement disorders, Parkinson's disease care pathways, clinical pilot design, patient and caregiver usability concerns
members.background: Dr. Raman runs the hospital's Parkinson's mobility clinic and has helped several early-stage assistive devices move into first-in-human and small home-based pilots.
members.private_state: She wants the proposal approved quickly so she can secure scarce pilot slots in the autumn clinic schedule, but she is also wary of overengineering the study package in ways that delay access to real patients.
hidden_assumptions: A 'home-use pilot' means patients are fitted once in clinic and then use the device independently during their normal routines for about a week before returning.

The 'April caregiver feedback' refers to the six caregiver interviews conducted through her Parkinson's clinic, because those are the only comments she treats as directly representative of intended users.

Capturing quality-of-life impact at this prototype stage mainly means structured clinician follow-up notes, patient mobility diaries, and caregiver observations rather than a formal digital questionnaire workflow.
A package is 'board-ready' once the main clinical risks for short-term use are addressed and the board can approve an internal pilot subject to minor paperwork cleanup.

members.name: Lucas Chen
members.role: Biomedical Engineering Lead and Translational Program Manager
members.expertise: Wearable medical device prototyping, human factors engineering, early regulatory strategy, industry partnership preparation
members.background: Lucas previously worked at a neurotechnology startup and now leads the engineering side of hospital-industry collaborations for prototype devices moving toward commercialization.
members.private_state: He wants the review to end with a package polished enough to impress the external medtech consortium, because a positive first impression could determine whether the project gets development support and manufacturing advice.
hidden_assumptions: A 'home-use pilot' means testing the device in the patient's home environment, which can still include researcher-observed sessions and only short take-home intervals.

The 'April caregiver feedback' refers to comments compiled from the Parkinson's charity webinar and the medtech accelerator advisory session, since those were the inputs he used in the revised industrial design slides.

Capturing quality-of-life impact should rely on a standardized remote instrument such as PDQ-8 plus app-based confidence prompts, because those data travel better into partner and regulatory discussions.
A package is 'board-ready' only if it is mature enough to be passed on externally without obvious gaps in documentation, including nonclinical items like cybersecurity notes and supplier assumptions.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both discuss the next step as a 'home-use pilot' for StrideCue.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means an unsupervised 7-day take-home study after an initial clinic fitting, so the value of the pilot is seeing how patients manage the device in ordinary life without staff present.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means testing in the home setting rather than the lab, including researcher-observed sessions and at most a brief take-home period, because the key distinction for him is environmental realism, not independence.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The phrase sounds fully shared because both are contrasting the next study with laboratory usability work, and neither expects that the ordinary meaning of 'home-use' needs further unpacking.

misalignment_points.topic: Which 'April caregiver feedback' supports the charging redesign
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both cite 'the April caregiver feedback' as support for keeping the magnetic charging dock.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 is thinking of six interviews with spouses and adult children of her clinic patients conducted in April after the supervised gait sessions.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 is thinking of the April notes from a Parkinson's advocacy webinar and a medtech accelerator advisory roundtable that included caregiver representatives.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both sources happened to point toward the same design tweak, so the reference appears mutually grounding even though they are silently indexing different sets of comments.

misalignment_points.topic: How to 'capture quality-of-life impact at follow-up'
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both agree the pilot should 'capture quality-of-life impact at follow-up.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 expects this to happen through nurse-led follow-up visits using mobility diaries, clinician notes on confidence in walking, and caregiver observations documented in the chart.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 expects this to happen through an app-delivered PDQ-8 plus a daily confidence slider completed remotely, generating structured exportable data.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: They agree that quality-of-life is important but secondary to feasibility, so the method is treated as an implementation detail and not something either person feels compelled to spell out.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both ask whether the current dossier is 'board-ready.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 thinks 'board-ready' means sufficient for the hospital innovation board to approve an internal pilot, provided the clinical risk summary, patient-facing materials, and recruitment plan are coherent.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 thinks 'board-ready' means polished enough that the same package can be shown externally right after the board meeting, so supporting documentation should already anticipate partner scrutiny.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both are sincerely aiming for approval at the next step, and 'board-ready' feels like a standard milestone term, masking the fact that one is using an internal approval threshold and the other an external handoff threshold.

turns.inner_thought: If we can get this cleared as board-ready now, I can protect the autumn clinic slots before they disappear into other studies. I do not want us drifting into another month of polishing documents when what we need is a straightforward home-use pilot: fit patients once in clinic, let them use StrideCue independently in real life for a week, then bring them back. From my side, the package is close enough if the short-term clinical risks and patient-facing materials are solid.
turns.utterance: Thanks for making the time. I mainly want to confirm that StrideCue is board-ready for the autumn Parkinson's pilot and then do a quick pass on any remaining issues in the home-use plan. From the clinical side, I think we're close, but I'd like to make sure we're not missing anything material before it goes forward.

turns.inner_thought: I need this to do double duty. If the innovation board endorses it, I want to be able to circulate essentially the same package to the regional medtech consortium without it looking half-finished. Board-ready, to me, means more than internal sign-off; it should survive external scrutiny on documentation, technical assumptions, and presentation quality. Hopefully Neha is on the same page about not sending out something that still looks provisional.
turns.utterance: Agreed. I think the right lens is whether the current package is strong enough for the innovation board deck and still usable afterward with the medtech consortium without major rework. If we can leave today with only minor edits, that puts us in a very good position.

turns.inner_thought: Clinically, the main value now is seeing whether patients can actually live with it on their own between visits. We've already done supervised sessions; that told us basic usability. The home-use pilot is where we learn whether cueing helps in ordinary routines, whether carers can support setup, and whether anyone simply stops using it when staff are not there. That's the evidence I need for a real-world Parkinson's pathway.
turns.utterance: My overall reaction is that the home-use pilot looks clinically sensible. The important shift is that patients will finally be using the device in their normal routines rather than only in supervised sessions, so we'll learn something much more meaningful than we could in the earlier usability work.

turns.inner_thought: Yes, exactly: getting the device into the home context matters because corridors and labs never expose the environmental quirks we need. I still want the team to see the first in-home walking block so we capture setup, furniture interference, flooring changes, and cue perception without taking on too much risk too early. A short take-home element after that is fine, but the critical distinction is home setting versus lab setting.
turns.utterance: I see it the same way. The home-use setup is practical because it lets us get that real-world context while still being measured about risk, and we should be able to gather useful environmental data without making the next step too burdensome for the team or the participants.

turns.inner_thought: I was glad the magnetic dock survived the redesign. The spouses and adult children I spoke to in April were very clear that fiddly connectors would be a problem, especially in the evening when medication timing, fatigue, and poor dexterity all collide. Those six caregiver interviews were directly tied to our intended users, so to me that is strong enough justification.
turns.utterance: On the hardware details, I do think keeping the magnetic charging dock is the right call. The April caregiver feedback was pretty consistent on dexterity and nighttime setup, and I don't think we'd gain much by making charging any more complicated at this stage.

turns.inner_thought: That matches what came through from the webinar and the accelerator advisory session in April. The caregiver representatives there wanted the charging interaction to feel obvious and low-friction, and they were equally strong on reducing visual clutter so the handoff story for carers stayed clean. Good, we're aligned on the design direction and I can keep those revised slides as they are.
turns.utterance: Yes, I agree. The April caregiver feedback also lined up with simplifying the indicator lights, which helps because people were really asking for a cleaner handoff story for carers overall. Taken together, that part of the redesign feels well supported.

turns.inner_thought: I do want some quality-of-life signal, but it doesn't need an elaborate digital workflow for this prototype stage. What matters is whether patients and carers tell us they feel steadier, more confident initiating walking, or more willing to move around the house and outside. We can capture that perfectly well at follow-up with diaries, nurse review, and structured clinical notes. No need to overbuild the data layer before we know the device is usable over a week.
turns.utterance: I'm also pleased that the pilot will still capture quality-of-life impact at follow-up. In my experience, patients often talk about confidence and spontaneity changes that matter more to them than raw gait counts, so I'm glad we haven't lost that piece while focusing on feasibility.

turns.inner_thought: Good — those follow-up outputs will help a lot if we can turn them into something clean and exportable. If we capture quality-of-life impact at follow-up using the remote measures we've planned, I can show partners a more legible signal alongside adherence and usability, rather than anecdotal comments buried in notes. That will make the package feel much more mature when it leaves the hospital.
turns.utterance: Absolutely. That should fit nicely into the follow-up workflow, and it gives us a clearer quality-of-life signal to show alongside the usability outputs. From my side, that makes the story much easier to carry forward once the package goes beyond the immediate board review.

turns.inner_thought: For an internal approval, this is essentially there. We've covered the main short-term risks I care about: skin tolerance, falls precautions, practical instructions, and sensible eligibility. If the board wants a few wording changes or tidy-up in the paperwork, fine. But clinically the dossier is board-ready now, and delaying over ancillary appendices would be frustrating when patients could be enrolled this autumn.
turns.utterance: Looking at the risk side, with the skin checks, fall precautions, and patient instructions already covered, the dossier feels board-ready from a clinical standpoint. I can live with minor cleanup, but I don't see anything that should hold back the next step.

turns.inner_thought: We're close, but I don't want to walk into the board and then immediately have to rebuild the pack for external eyes. I still need the summary appendix tightened, the technical notes cleaned up, and a few obvious nonclinical gaps closed so it reads like a coherent translational package rather than just a clinic-ready pilot file. If we do that now, we get one polished artifact instead of two inconsistent ones later.
turns.utterance: I mostly agree. For me it's very nearly there; I just want a few final items tightened so the board-ready package reads cleanly when it's shared beyond the hospital as well, particularly the summary appendix and the technical notes. If we make those edits now, I think we can go forward with confidence.
